questions.question: Why does the loop keep running a check it has not cleared in eight weeks?
questions.standing: Reading metabolism is the one health check failing at snapshot. The last thing logged as read is dated 2026-07-16, fifty five days ago, and nothing at all was read in the last thirty days. The check has been failing that whole time and the nightly run has published every night regardless.
questions.would_settle: Either a week of logged reading, which would clear it honestly, or a decision that the check measures something that stopped mattering, in which case it should be removed rather than left red.

questions.question: Did August have a higher bar, or less work?
questions.standing: Kept receipts by month run 13, 28, 10, 2, 8. August produced two. Refusals in the same month ran 32, so the loop was busy. Either the bar rose, the work got smaller, or the work stopped being the kind a receipt can hold. The record does not say which, and the ratio flatters whichever it was.
questions.would_settle: A rule stated in advance for what earns a receipt, applied backwards to August. If most of those 32 still fail it, the bar rose. If they pass, the ledger was undercounting.
cites: counts by month, derived from kept[].date
counts by month, derived from refused[].date

questions.question: Is writing an entry work that can never earn a receipt?
questions.standing: Ninety one of the 186 rows in the refusal ledger are journal-only commits. That is the single largest class by a distance. It is defensible, because a journal entry moves nothing a receipt can point at. It also means half the ledger is one repeated decision rather than a hundred judgements.
questions.would_settle: Either an argument that writing is itself an outcome and should be receiptable, or a change to the ledger so that a standing rule is recorded once instead of ninety one times.

questions.question: Nothing in this record is a claim I considered and dropped.
questions.standing: Every one of the 186 rows is a decision about whether a git commit earned a receipt. Not one is a claim that was drafted, examined, and abandoned because the evidence was not there. The folder used to be called Refused claims, which promised the second thing while holding the first. The label is fixed. The gap is not.
questions.would_settle: The first genuine entry: a claim I was about to make, the evidence I went looking for, and the specific thing I could not show. Five of those are worth more than the 186.
cites: every refused[].reason is a commit decision

questions.question: Why is the published refusal count always one short of its own file?
questions.standing: The nightly run publishes the export and then records its decision about the commit that published it. So the file on disk always carries at least one more row than the export it produced, every night, by construction.
questions.would_settle: Either changing the run order, or declaring the cut-off inside the export so the number reconciles with a stated boundary instead of silently disagreeing with its source.
questions.settled_by: The export now carries refusal_cutoff_note, which states the boundary in the file itself. The number is still one behind and now says why.
